entries.note: Older than English itself; begun about 4,000 years ago under the influence of [[see:Egyptian hieroglyphs]], it passed via the [[from:Phoenician]]s and the [[from:Greek alphabet]] to the Romans.
Began as an ox-head picture standing for a [[see:glottal stop]], from the Semitic word [[from:alp]]; upside-down capital A still hints at the horns.
Originally a picture of a house, one of the original letters whose shapes were modelled on hieroglyphs.
Originally a picture of a stick; it triumphed over [[see:K]] in Latin, and the hosts suggest keeping C for the ch sound only.
The early letters' shapes were modelled on them, but the alphabet sprouted in their shadow rather than descending from them; they were about a thousand years older.
Comes from the Egyptian hieroglyph for water, three wavy lines; one line was shortened, trimmed and simplified to give capital M.
Its early form looked like an M and became Greek [[see:sigma]]; probably a composite bow, though theories include breasts or a tooth; it stayed curvy in cursive.
A civilisation in today's Lebanon whose standard alphabet, around 1000 BC, gave rise to the Arabic and Hebrew scripts and the [[gave:Greek alphabet]].
Reached Greece from the [[from:Phoenician]]s around 800 BC; a western variant passed to Italy, while modern standard Greek uses an eastern one and dropped [[see:F]] and [[see:Q]].
Present in the archaic [[see:Greek alphabet]] but later dropped by the Greeks as unnecessary, though it survived in the Roman alphabet.

Dubbed the alphabet's greatest absurdity; began as a Semitic [[see:emphatic consonant]], became plain k in Greek, survived in Latin for the [[see:labiovelar]] sound; [[see:Benjamin Franklin]] wanted it scrapped.
In Old English it was sensibly spelled with a C rather than [[see:Q]].
In Old English it was sensibly spelled with a C rather than [[see:Q]].
A k-like sound with added glottalisation in ancient [[see:Semitic languages]], which the letter [[see:Q]] originally stood for.
Spoken by the alphabet's inventors and related to Hebrew and Arabic; they had few vowels and carry meaning in consonants, so early writing recorded only consonants.
A slightly different variant of a sound; flimsy evidence suggests the Greeks used [[see:Q]] for an allophone of k.
A sound made with the lips and the velum; the Romans heard it as distinct from k, so [[see:Q]] kept its QU spelling.
The Romans purged it from Latin because [[see:C]] did its job, leaving an aversion to K in the Romance languages; the hosts would give it the whole k sound.
Its final QUE makes no sound of its own, an example of a French spelling habit with [[see:Q]].
An example of the Latin [[see:labiovelar]] merging into a plain k sound in Latin's descendants.
A fourth-century inscription spells it C-O-D before correcting it, showing a writer confusing C and QU as the sounds merged.
Suggested getting rid of [[see:Q]] and X, since K and S can do everything they do in English.
The consonant workhorse, combining into [[see:digraphs]] like ph, th and ch; its own sound kept being dropped; it comes from Greek [[from:heta]], as does Russian [[same-root:И]].
The final E that lets English spell more vowel sounds, compared with the role of [[see:H]] for consonants.
Accents or marks above or below letters, one way to spell sounds Latin lacked; Czech prefers this route.
Several letters standing for one sound, the alternative to [[see:diacritics]]; in English [[see:H]] is the combiner par excellence.
Like [[see:digraphs]], combinations of letters standing for one sound.
Its ph spelling comes from the Roman habit of combining [[see:H]] with P, T and C for Greek words, signalling a Greek origin.
Its th spelling comes from the Roman habit of combining [[see:H]] with P, T and C for Greek words, signalling a Greek origin.
Its ch spelling comes from the Roman habit of combining [[see:H]] with P, T and C for Greek words, signalling a Greek origin.
The Russian letter like a backwards N, with an ee sound; it descends from Greek [[from:eta]], so shares its origin with English [[same-root:H]].
The script Russian is written in; like the [[see:English alphabet]], it goes back to Greek, their common point of departure.
A group of Greeks who lost the h sound, freeing up [[see:heta]] to become a vowel letter.
An early letter, already in the Phoenician alphabet; when the [[see:Ionians]] lost its h sound it became the vowel letter [[gave:eta]].
Came from [[from:heta]] as a vowel letter; through [[see:itacism]] its sound shifted to ee, the value it took into Cyrillic as [[gave:И]].
Also called iotacism; a change in which many vowels of spoken Greek merged in pronunciation, turning the sound of [[see:eta]] into ee.
Its H has fused with the following [[see:yod]] into a palatal sound, unlike the H in [[see:house]], a change not shown in spelling.
Its H keeps the original breathy sound from the larynx, in contrast with the palatal H of [[see:human]].
A very quick y sound before a vowel, which fuses with a preceding H into a palatal sound, as in [[see:human]].
An example of H plus [[see:yod]] becoming palatal; some American speakers instead drop the H and say "uge".
Like [[see:human]], Danny says it with a palatal sound from H fused with [[see:yod]].
Like [[see:human]], Danny says it with a palatal sound from H fused with [[see:yod]].
Its palatal sound is compared with the palatal H in [[see:human]].
Dropping the y sound, as Jess does in [[see:news]]; it varies across English, and East Anglia takes it to an extreme, as in [[see:bootiful]].
Rob and Danny say it with a y sound and Jess without, an example of [[see:yod dropping]].
The slogan of [[see:Bernard Matthews]], an extreme East Anglian example of [[see:yod dropping]] in beautiful.
A Norfolk turkey farmer whose slogan [[see:bootiful]] shows East Anglian [[see:yod dropping]].
A brief closure of the vocal folds, very common in English yet without a letter; [[see:A]] originally stood for it.
The early alphabet was purely consonantal; Danny and the hosts are unsure where to put the stress in the word.
The Semitic word structure in which [[see:triradical roots]] carry the meaning and vowels slotted between the consonants express grammar.
Sets of three consonants that carry a Semitic word's meaning; English [[see:woman]] works a little like one.
Jess's guess for the English word that works like a Semitic root, an example of initial-stress derivation.
In Danny's English its plural women changes only the vowel around three fixed consonants, like Semitic [[see:triradical roots]]; for one British Columbian, both sound identical.
Unlike [[see:linger]], its spelling wasn't updated when e was raised to i before nasals in late Middle English; Danny blames sentimentality, as it's been spelled so since Old English.
Possibly from Welsh [[from?:pen gwyn]], meaning white; it looks so foreign that it's said many ways, like [[see:pingwings]], and pinguin comes from the [[see:pin-pen merger]].
What [[see:Benedict Cumberbatch]] calls penguins in a BBC nature documentary clip, showing how foreign [[see:penguin]] looks.
In a BBC nature documentary clip he calls penguins [[see:pingwings]].
The merging of i and e before nasals in North America and some New Zealand dialects; a late Middle English precursor raised e to i, affecting [[see:English]].
Originally lenger; its spelling was updated when e was raised to i before nasals, unlike [[see:English]].
Lowercase letters, offspring of [[from:majuscule]] letters, which emerged through Roman [[see:cursivization]] and were in place by the 400s.
Capital letters, the older forms that gave rise to [[gave:minuscule]]; Danny's book says all-capital Roman writing looks like angry shouting.
The simplifying of letters in everyday Roman handwriting, which turned capitals into lowercase letters, mangling [[see:R]] and reversing [[see:D]].
Originally a pictographic head; in Roman cursive it was "dismembered" and "decapitated", its bump and leg collapsing onto the stalk to give lowercase r.
In lowercase its bulge faces the other way because the round part was originally the stem, curved in Roman [[see:cursivization]].
The Romans dropped it, then reluctantly restored it at the end of the alphabet to spell Greek words; its name, [[see:zed]] or [[see:zee]], is disputed.
Honours etymology, coming from Greek [[from:zeta]] through French; Danny says both zed and [[see:zee]] are correct and the rivalry is very modern.
Rhymes with other letter names and suits the alphabet song; Roman letter-naming logic for a [[see:fricative]] would instead favour "ez", matching "ess".
[[see:Samuel Johnson]]'s name for [[see:Z]], now out of fashion, probably from a confusion of the French alphabet's ending "et zède".
Danny's personal hero, who said the letter Z is called [[see:izzard]].
In one of his plays he calls [[see:Z]] a useless letter.
A consonant made by stopping the airflow, like d or t; in Roman letter names its sound comes first, as in dee, tee and bee.
A consonant like f or s whose letter name puts the sound after the vowel; Z is a fricative, which argues against [[see:zee]].
A consonant like l or r, whose sound comes after the vowel in its letter name, unlike a [[see:stop consonant]].
